evidence.citation: Cotrimoxazole as prophylaxis against opportunistic infections in HIV‐infected Zambian children (CHAP): a double‐blind randomised placebo‐controlled trial
evidence.population: Children aged 1–14 years with clinical features of HIV infection in Zambia; 541 randomized, 7 subsequently identified as HIV-negative and excluded (HIV-infected children analyzed).
evidence.setting: Zambia; resource-poor setting with high levels of bacterial resistance to co-trimoxazole; pediatric outpatient/clinical trial context.
evidence.intervention: Daily co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) prophylaxis; dosing not specified in abstract.

outcomes.outcome_name: All-cause mortality among children followed beyond 12 months (n=320)
Severe adverse events (grade 3 or 4) — comparative incidence
Neutrophil count <0.5×10^9/L (on one occasion) — comparative incidence
Pneumocystis carinii detection among children with pneumonia (nasopharyngeal aspirates)

evidence.study_design: Double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial (RCT); analysis by intention-to-treat; early stopping by DSMC.
evidence.follow_up: Median follow-up 19 months; subgroup analysis for >12 months (n=320).
adverse_events: Grade 3 or 4 adverse events: 16/ (6%) co-trimoxazole vs 18/ (7%) placebo.
Neutrophil count <0.5×10^9/L on one occasion: 16 (6%) co-trimoxazole vs 7 (3%) placebo; p=0.06.
key_findings: Mortality: 74 deaths (28%) in co-trimoxazole vs 112 deaths (42%) in placebo; HR 0.57 (95% CI 0.43–0.77), p=0.0002.
Mortality benefit persisted beyond 12 months: HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.27–0.84) among n=320 followed >12 months; test for heterogeneity p=0.60.
Effect consistent across ages (test for heterogeneity p=0.82) and baseline CD4 counts (test for heterogeneity p=0.36).
Severe (grade 3/4) adverse events similar between groups: 6% co-trimoxazole vs 7% placebo.
Pneumocystis carinii detected by immunofluorescence in 1/73 nasopharyngeal aspirates (placebo group) among children with pneumonia.
evidence.notes: Trial conducted in Zambia with high background bacterial resistance to co-trimoxazole; early stopping recommended by DSMC in Oct 2003; daily prophylaxis regimen; intention-to-treat analysis; placebo-controlled; double-blind.

quality_assessment.citation: Cotrimoxazole as prophylaxis against opportunistic infections in HIV‐infected Zambian children (CHAP): a double‐blind randomised placebo‐controlled trial
strengths: Large relative reduction in all-cause mortality with reasonably tight confidence intervals
Effects consistent across age groups and baseline CD4 strata
Conducted in a high-burden, resource-limited setting with high background bacterial resistance
limitations: Early stopping by Data and Safety Monitoring Committee, which can overestimate treatment effects
Sequence generation and allocation concealment not fully detailed in the abstract
Dosing regimen not specified in the abstract
No detailed reporting of illness episode counts; primary focus on mortality and severe adverse events
Single-country study; external generalizability beyond similar settings uncertain
Borderline higher severe neutropenia (p=0.06) suggests possible hematologic toxicity
Likely pre-ART or limited ART access context; applicability to ART-era programs uncertain
risk_of_bias_concerns: Insufficient reporting of allocation concealment in the abstract
Minor enrollment misclassification (7 later found HIV-negative and excluded from HIV-infected analysis)

synthesis: One double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial in Zambia evaluated daily cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV-infected children aged 1–14 years [1]. Despite high background bacterial resistance, cotrimoxazole significantly reduced all-cause mortality compared with placebo over a median 19 months. Event counts were 74 deaths in cotrimoxazole versus 112 in placebo. The mortality benefit persisted among children followed beyond 12 months (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.27–0.84) [1]. Benefits were consistent across age groups and baseline CD4 strata, suggesting broad efficacy across pediatric subgroups within the trial [1]. Illness episodes were not systematically quantified in the abstracted data; the focus was mortality and severe adverse events. Thus, direct estimates on non-fatal morbidity were not reported. Safety was generally comparable between groups. Grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 16 children (6%) on cotrimoxazole versus 18 (7%) on placebo. Severe neutropenia (<0.5×10^9/L on one occasion) occurred in 16 (6%) vs 7 (3%); p=0.06, indicating a borderline hematologic signal. No included study directly evaluated routine cotrimoxazole in infants of HIV-infected mothers (e.g., HIV-exposed uninfected infants); applicability to that group is therefore indirect within this evidence set. The trial was conducted in a resource-limited setting with high antimicrobial resistance, supporting relevance where bacterial infections are common. However, early stopping by the DSMC may inflate effect estimates, and the pre-ART or limited ART context reduces certainty about generalizability to current programs with widespread ART access [1]. Implications for practice in low-resource settings: Where ART access is limited or bacterial infection burden is high, routine cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV-infected children is likely to reduce mortality with acceptable safety. Programs should monitor for hematologic toxicity (e.g., neutropenia) and reassess benefits as ART coverage and epidemiology evolve.
limitations: Single RCT from one country and one health-system context
Early stopping for benefit may overestimate treatment effect
Limited reporting of allocation concealment and dosing details in abstract
Lack of detailed illness episode outcomes; focus on mortality and severe adverse events
Pre-ART or limited ART context; applicability to current ART-era settings uncertain
No direct evidence for infants of HIV-infected mothers within the included studies
Setting with high local resistance may not reflect all regions
